explanation: A node can be inserted only after its ancestors, but available nodes from different subtrees may be interleaved freely. Backtrack over a frontier of nodes whose parents are already chosen: select one, append its value, remove it from the frontier and add its children. This enumerates the valid ancestor-before-descendant orders directly.
correctness: Every generated order begins with root and exposes a child only after its parent is chosen, so every ancestor precedes its descendants. Distinct BST value ranges route each later insertion into the same ancestor-defined subtree, hence any such order recreates the original tree. Conversely, an insertion order creating that tree must place every node after its ancestors; at each step its next node is therefore in the backtracking frontier and that branch is explored. Unique chosen-node sequences cannot repeat because their first differing frontier choice gives a different next distinct value. An empty frontier emits one complete row, including the single empty row for an empty tree.
walkthrough: For root 2 with left child 1 and right child 3, root must be first. Both children then become available, yielding [2,1,3] and [2,3,1]. These are the two accepted rows, in either outer order. [1,2,3] instead creates root 1 and is invalid.
timeComplexity: O(S*(n+1)^2) conservative time for S returned sequences of n values: copying a frontier of at most n at each of n choices on each complete search path. Output alone needs O(S*n+1).
spaceComplexity: O(S*n) returned values plus O(n^2) frontier copies along one recursion path and O(n) value/path frames. n<=8 bounds the combinatorial output.
edgeCases: Empty tree returns [[]], leaf and chain with a single sequence.
Balanced branches with many interleavings, arbitrary outer order, duplicate-row rejection and signed endpoints.
